title: Hannah's Song and the Corrupt House of Eli
summary: Hannah praises the LORD in a song that celebrates his holiness and his power to overturn human fortunes, raising the poor and humbling the proud, and ends by looking toward the LORD's king, his anointed. The narrative then contrasts the boy Samuel, faithfully serving at Shiloh, with Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas, who abuse the sacrifices and the women at the sanctuary. Eli rebukes them weakly, and a man of God announces that Eli's priestly house will be cut down and replaced by a faithful priest.
story: Chapter 1 ended with Hannah handing her son to Eli at Shiloh. Chapter 2 opens with her response, not a lament but a song of triumph, and then turns sharply to the priesthood Samuel has been placed in. The chapter sets up a contrast that will drive the next several chapters: the humble family that gives to God and the priestly family that takes from him. Eli's sons will die in chapter 4, the ark will be captured, and the priesthood of Shiloh will collapse, while the boy growing up in the middle of that corruption will become the prophet through whom God speaks again. Hannah's song also looks much further ahead, to a king who does not yet exist.
historical:
Priests in Israel were descended from Aaron, and Eli's family held the priesthood at Shiloh. The man of God traces their calling back to the time in Egypt. The judgment he announces unfolds in stages across Israel's history. Hophni and Phinehas die on one day in 1 Samuel 4. Later Saul massacres the priests of Nob, who are Eli's descendants (1 Samuel 22), leaving only Abiathar. When Solomon becomes king he removes Abiathar from the priesthood, and 1 Kings 2:27 says this fulfilled the word the LORD had spoken at Shiloh concerning the house of Eli. Zadok, who served alongside Abiathar under David, became the leading priest in Solomon's temple, and his descendants held that office for centuries. Many interpreters therefore identify Zadok and his line as the faithful priest of verse 35, though some see Samuel as a first fulfillment.

The song itself raises a historical question. It speaks of a king and his anointed, though Israel had no king in Hannah's day. Some scholars think an existing royal psalm was placed in her mouth by the book's author because it suited the moment; others hold that Hannah spoke prophetically. Either way, the song functions in its present place as an overture to the whole book of Samuel.
cultural:
Israel's law carefully regulated the priests' share of offerings. The fat of a peace offering belonged to the LORD and had to be burned on the altar first (Leviticus 3:16; 7:23-25), and the priest received specified portions, such as the breast and right thigh (Leviticus 7:31-34). Eli's sons violate both rules. They take whatever the fork brings up from the pot, then demand raw meat before the fat is even burned, and they threaten force. In a culture where most people rarely ate meat except at sacrifices, this was both a sacrilege against God and a theft from worshipers.

The women who served at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting are also mentioned in Exodus 38:8, though their exact role is unknown. The sons' sexual abuse of them turns the sanctuary into something like the fertility shrines of Canaan. Samuel's linen ephod was a simple priestly garment, distinct from the high priest's ornate ephod, and Hannah's yearly gift of a little robe shows a mother's continuing care. The word horn in Hannah's song draws on the image of a wild ox holding its head high; to have one's horn exalted meant strength, honor, and victory.
literary: Hannah's song (verses 1-10) is Hebrew poetry built on parallel lines and sharp contrasts: the mighty and the feeble, the full and the hungry, the barren and the mother of many, death and life, poverty and wealth. It moves from personal praise to a description of God's character and ends with his judgment of the earth and his king. The second half of the book of Samuel closes with another song, David's in 2 Samuel 22, which shares many of the same images (rock, horn, the LORD thundering from heaven, the anointed); many scholars see the two songs as deliberate bookends. The narrative after the song alternates between Eli's sons and Samuel in short, contrasting paragraphs: the sons' sin (12-17), Samuel ministering (18-21), the sons' sin again (22-25), Samuel growing (26). The prophecy of verses 27-36 then pronounces judgment. The narrator's comment that the sons would not listen “since the LORD intended to put them to death” (verse 25) is one of the chapter's hardest lines.

outline.t: Hannah's song: the LORD who raises and brings low
The contempt of Eli's sons for the offerings
Samuel serves; Hannah is blessed with more children
Eli's feeble rebuke and Samuel's growth
A man of God announces judgment on Eli's house

doctrines.note: Hannah's song is one of the Bible's great statements of God's rule over human life: “The LORD brings death and gives life; He brings down to Sheol and raises up” (verse 6). No human power is secure, and no one is beyond his lifting.

The song's final line speaks of the LORD's anointed, the first use of the word messiah for a king in the Bible. It shapes the hope that runs through the rest of Samuel and the Prophets: a king anointed by God who will rule under him.

“There is no one holy like the LORD” (verse 2). Eli's sons treat holy things with contempt, and the chapter shows that God's holiness is not a neutral fact but a claim on those who serve him: “I will honor those who honor Me, but those who despise Me will be disdained” (verse 30).

God's judgment of Eli's house is announced long before it falls. It shows that privilege in religious office brings greater accountability, and that God will not let his worship be used for personal gain indefinitely.

words.note: Mashiach, anointed. It describes someone set apart by being anointed with oil, used of priests and especially of kings. Here it names the king the LORD will strengthen, and in verse 35 the king before whom the faithful priest will serve. Transliterated through Greek and Latin it gives the English Messiah, and translated into Greek it gives Christ.

Qeren, horn. The horn of an animal was a natural symbol of strength. The song opens with Hannah's horn exalted and closes with the horn of the LORD's anointed exalted, so the personal vindication of one woman frames the future strength of Israel's king.

Tsur, rock. A common title for God in Hebrew poetry (see Deuteronomy 32), picturing him as a place of refuge, stability, and protection. Hannah says there is no Rock like our God, setting him above every other source of security.

Kavod, glory or honor. The root means weight, and the chapter plays on it: God raises the poor to a throne of honor (verse 8), Eli honors his sons more than God, the sons fatten themselves, and God says he will honor those who honor him (verse 30). The same root returns in chapter 4, when the glory departs from Israel and Eli, being heavy, falls to his death.

christ: Hannah's song is the direct model for Mary's song in Luke 1:46-55. Both women rejoice in God as savior, and both celebrate a God who humbles the proud, lifts the lowly, and fills the hungry. Luke clearly wants readers to hear Hannah behind Mary: the birth of Jesus is the greatest of the reversals Hannah sang about. The song's closing reference to the LORD's anointed opens the Bible's line of messianic hope, which the New Testament sees fulfilled in Jesus, the Christ, the anointed King. The promise of a faithful priest who does what is in God's heart and mind also resonates with the New Testament's picture of Christ as the faithful high priest (Hebrews 2:17; 3:1-2), though in its original setting the verse points first to a human priestly line, and the connection to Christ is thematic rather than direct prediction.

hard.q: What does it mean that Eli's sons would not listen “since the LORD intended to put them to death”?
hard.a: The verse seems to say that God's purpose to judge the sons was the reason they ignored their father, which raises the question of whether they were responsible. Readers have answered in several ways. Many see here the same pattern as the hardening of Pharaoh in Exodus: after persistent, deliberate sin, God confirms people in the course they have chosen, so their refusal is both their own act and part of his judgment. Others stress that the Hebrew can be read more loosely (they didn't listen, for the LORD was pleased to put them to death), describing the outcome rather than a cause. Still others read it as the narrator's way of saying that the time for repentance had passed. On every reading, the text holds the sons fully accountable: their sin is described in detail, called very great, and treated as contempt for the LORD. The Bible regularly holds together God's sovereignty over judgment and human responsibility for sin without explaining how they fit, and this verse is one example.

questions: Hannah's song says God raises the poor and humbles the proud. Where do you see that pattern in Scripture, in history, or in your own life?
Eli rebuked his sons but did not stop them. What is the difference between disapproving of wrong and actually restraining it, especially for those with authority?
“I will honor those who honor Me” (verse 30). What does it look like to honor God in ordinary work and worship rather than using religion for personal gain?
